alarms.title: Alarms, and how they differ from problems
alarms.summary: A CloudWatch alarm is your rule. An OpsWatch problem is what OpsWatch measured. Both matter.
alarms.what: OpsWatch reads every CloudWatch alarm in the account and region you are looking at, and shows what each one watches rather than what it is called. It never changes an alarm, and it never treats one as a problem of its own.

before.0: A connected AWS account whose permission test passes.
before.1: At least one CloudWatch alarm. OpsWatch creates none.

0.title: Read the summary first
0.body: The bar at the top counts every alarm by state. In alarm, OK, and insufficient data are three separate counts — an alarm AWS could not evaluate is never added to OK.

1.title: Narrow by state, then by service
1.body: The state tabs and the service chips are links, so a filtered view can be shared and the back button works. Services come from the alarm’s namespace, never from its name.

2.title: Read a row
2.body: Each row leads with what is watched and where — “CPU on redis-prod” — and keeps the AWS alarm name underneath, because that is what your runbook and the console say.

3.title: Open one
3.body: The detail page explains the condition in full: metric, statistic, threshold, period, how many datapoints must breach, and what AWS does when data is missing.

alarms.verify: The counts at the top add up to the number of alarms you have, and every row names a metric and a resource rather than only an alarm name.

0.q: What is the difference between an alarm and a problem?
0.a: An alarm is a rule somebody wrote in AWS: a threshold on a metric. A problem is something OpsWatch decided was worth your attention, using its own detectors and evidence. An alarm in ALARM state does open a problem — but OpsWatch will never invent causes for it, because the rule is yours and it never saw your reasoning.

1.q: Why can I not see the alarm’s history?
1.a: Reading state transitions needs cloudwatch:DescribeAlarmHistory, which the read-only role does not ask for. Adding it would mean a new template version and every installation redeploying, so it is not granted for one page.

2.a: Target-tracking alarms fire as part of normal autoscaling. Counting them would make every scaling estate look permanently alarmed, so they are excluded until you ask for them.

3.q: The value shown is not the current value.
3.a: It is the datapoint AWS quoted when it last changed the state, which may be hours old. OpsWatch labels it as what AWS reported and does not pay for a second metric call to guess at “now”.

alerts.title: Alerts and notifications
alerts.summary: Rules turn problems into notifications, with a cooldown so nobody is paged twice.
alerts.what: A problem is something OpsWatch measured. An alert rule decides which problems are worth telling somebody about, and where to send them.

before.0: At least one connected account producing problems.

0.title: Look at the rules you already have
0.body: Alert rules. OpsWatch ships a starting set, and a rule you delete stays deleted even when a later version adds new ones.

1.title: Understand the cooldown
1.body: A rule that has fired will not fire again for the same subject until its cooldown passes. A flapping service does not become a flapping phone.

2.title: Acknowledge means a person has seen it
2.body: It stops the noise. It does not close the problem — only three consecutive clear readings do that.

3.title: Choose a destination
3.body: Settings, then Notifications. A webhook posts a signed JSON body to a URL you control. The page tells you what it will send and lets you send a test before you rely on it.

4.title: Turn on the weekly summary, if you want one
4.body: Settings, then Notifications. One summary a week, per environment, to the same destinations. It is off unless you switch it on, and it carries counts and a link — never a log line.

alerts.verify: Send a test notification from the destination you configured and confirm it arrives. The audit log records that it was sent.

0.q: What exactly is in the webhook body?
0.a: The problem, its severity, its subject and a link back into OpsWatch. Never a credential. The settings page shows an example payload.

1.q: A delivery failed.
1.a: OpsWatch retries with a backoff and records the failure. A destination that keeps failing is shown as failing rather than quietly dropped.

2.q: How do I verify a webhook really came from OpsWatch?
2.a: Each request is signed with the shared secret shown when you create the destination. Verify the signature before you act on the body.

3.q: Will OpsWatch send me anything I did not ask for?
3.a: No. With no destination nothing is ever sent, and the weekly summary is off until you switch it on. When it is on it goes out once a week, to the destinations you created and enabled, and it carries counts and a link — not the log lines behind them.

aws-permissions.title: AWS permissions: what OpsWatch reads, and what it cannot do
aws-permissions.summary: Every action in the policy, why it is there, and how to change your mind.
aws-permissions.what: The role OpsWatch asks for contains read actions only. This is the list, grouped the way the permission test groups it, so you can check the two against each other.

before.0: A connected AWS account.

0.title: Describe calls: what exists
0.body: ECS, EC2, load balancers and RDS describe actions tell OpsWatch which resources you have. They return configuration, never data.

1.title: CloudWatch: what they are doing
1.body: GetMetricData and ListMetrics read the metrics AWS already publishes. ListMetrics is also how OpsWatch discovers Redis and Kubernetes without asking for more permissions. GetMetricData is the one AWS bills for, and OpsWatch caps how often it runs.

2.title: Logs: only when you ask
2.body: Log groups are listed so you can pick one. Queries run when you run them, and the cost is stated beside the button.

3.title: Changing your mind
3.body: Update the stack from the connection page. OpsWatch tells you when the template it generated has moved on from the one you deployed.

aws-permissions.verify: Run the permission test on the connection. Every service you expect shows as allowed; anything else is named with the exact action.

0.q: I want to grant less than the template asks for.
0.a: You can. Remove the actions you do not want and redeploy — the permission test will show those services as denied, and the pages that need them will say so rather than showing you an empty screen.

1.q: Does OpsWatch store my AWS credentials?
1.a: For a role, there is nothing to store: OpsWatch assumes the role each time. For access keys, they are encrypted with your OPSWATCH_SECRET and never returned to a browser.

checkup.title: Checkup: what is worth fixing
checkup.summary: A review of configuration, separate from the problems that are happening now.
checkup.what: Checkup looks at how your estate is set up rather than at what it is doing. It finds the things that will bite later — a service with one task, a database with no backups configured, telemetry that is switched off.

before.0: A connected AWS account that has passed its permission test.

0.title: Open Checkup
0.body: Overview, then Checkup. It reads what it already collected, so it costs nothing to open.

1.title: Read a finding
1.body: Each one says what it saw, why that matters and what to do. Findings are not problems: nothing is on fire.

2.title: Decide
2.body: Some findings are deliberate choices. OpsWatch does not nag, and it never changes anything.

checkup.verify: Checkup lists findings or says plainly that it has nothing to report — and tells you when it last looked.

0.q: What is the difference between a finding, a problem, an alarm and an error?
0.a: A finding is about configuration. A problem is about behaviour OpsWatch measured. An alarm is a CloudWatch rule you wrote. An error is an exception from your application. They are four different things and OpsWatch keeps them apart.

1.q: Does OpsWatch audit my Google account?
1.a: No. Google is only a way to sign in to OpsWatch. There is no Google audit.

0.label: Keep history, so findings have a baseline

cloudflare.title: Connect Cloudflare
cloudflare.summary: Traffic, cache and threats at the edge, for the zones you choose.
cloudflare.what: Cloudflare sees the requests that never reach your origin: the ones it cached, the ones it blocked, and the ones it could not serve. Connecting it tells you what happened in front of AWS.

before.0: A Cloudflare account with at least one zone.
before.1: Permission to create an API token on it.

0.title: Create a read-only token
0.body: In your Cloudflare dashboard, create an API token with Zone read and Analytics read for the zones you want. Do not use a global API key.

1.title: Paste it into OpsWatch
1.body: Settings, then Cloudflare. The token is encrypted before it is stored and is never sent back to a browser — not even to the page you pasted it into.

2.title: Verify it
2.body: Verification calls Cloudflare and lists the zones the token can actually read. A saved token is not a working one, and OpsWatch shows the difference.

3.title: Choose zones
3.body: A verified token watching no zone reads nothing, so choosing is part of connecting rather than a step after it.

cloudflare.verify: The Cloudflare page shows requests, cache hit ratio, origin errors and threats for each zone you selected, with the day they were measured.

0.q: Verification failed.
0.a: OpsWatch shows the error code Cloudflare returned rather than a guess. The usual causes are a token without analytics permission or one scoped to a different zone.

1.q: The numbers are a day behind.
1.a: They are daily rollups from Cloudflare’s analytics. OpsWatch says which day each figure belongs to instead of implying it is live.

2.q: Can I replace the token without losing my zone selection?
2.a: Yes. Replacing the credential keeps the connection; only the token changes, and it is verified again.

0.label: Let a model narrate what was measured

connect-aws.title: Connect an AWS account
connect-aws.summary: A read-only IAM role, deployed by a CloudFormation template OpsWatch generates for you.
connect-aws.what: OpsWatch reads your AWS account through a role it is allowed to assume. The role is read-only, the template that creates it is generated for your account, and you can delete it at any time.

before.0: Permission to deploy a CloudFormation stack in the AWS account.
before.1: The AWS account number, twelve digits.
before.2: Which regions you want OpsWatch to read.

0.title: Add the connection
0.body: Connections, then Add a connection, then AWS. Give it a name you will recognise, the account number, and the regions. You can add as many AWS accounts as you like — production, staging, one per client — and each keeps its own data, its own alerts and its own permission status.

1.title: Choose IAM role
1.body: Access keys are offered for local testing and are marked as such. For anything real, use the role: OpsWatch assumes it, AWS records who assumed it, and you can revoke it in one place without changing anything in OpsWatch.

2.title: Deploy the template
2.body: Download it and run the command shown, or press Launch Stack if this installation has an S3 bucket configured. Either way it creates one IAM role with one read-only policy, and nothing else. The trust policy names OpsWatch’s own identity and an ExternalId unique to this connection, so the role cannot be assumed through another connection.

3.title: Confirm the role
3.body: OpsWatch has already worked the ARN out from the account, the region and the connection, so the field is filled in. Press Save. If you would rather check it against the stack, the command that reads the RoleArn output is one disclosure down.

4.title: Run the permission test
4.body: It calls one harmless read per service and tells you exactly which ones answered. This is the step that proves the role exists and works — everything before it is preparation.

connect-aws.verify: The connection shows Connected and the permission checklist shows each service as allowed. Anything denied is named, with the action that was refused.

0.q: The test says the role belongs to another account.
0.a: The ARN you pasted is from a different account number than the one on the connection. Check the twelve digits in the ARN.

1.q: Some services are denied.
1.a: That is fine and OpsWatch will keep working — it simply cannot read those. The checklist names each one so you can decide whether to add it.

2.q: Can OpsWatch change anything in my account?
2.a: No. The policy contains read actions only. It cannot deploy, scale, roll back or delete.

connect-github.title: Connect code
connect-github.summary: From a problem, to the deployment near it, to the commit, to the files that changed.
connect-github.what: When OpsWatch knows which repository a service is built from, it can show you what changed just before a problem started. It reads your code; it never writes to it.

before.0: A GitHub account with access to the repositories you want to link.
before.1: A connected AWS account, so there are services to map to.

0.title: Connect GitHub
0.body: Settings, then Repositories. Paste a token with read access to the repositories you care about. It is encrypted before it is stored and never sent back to a browser.

1.title: Choose repositories
1.body: Discover lists what the token can see. Import the ones you want; the rest are left alone.

2.title: Map a service to a repository
2.body: This is the link that makes the chain work. Without it OpsWatch knows a deployment happened and not what was in it.

3.title: Check deployment enrichment
3.body: Containers, then Deployments. An enriched deployment shows the commits it carried and how many files they touched.

4.title: Open code from a problem
4.body: On a problem with a nearby deployment, "what changed" takes you to the commit and the files. Where an error carries a stack frame, the link goes to that file at that commit.

connect-github.verify: A deployment shows its commits. A problem with a deployment near it offers the changed files. Both say plainly when a mapping is missing instead of showing nothing.

0.q: A deployment has no commits.
0.a: The service is not mapped to a repository, or the commit it deployed is not in the repository OpsWatch has. The deployment page says which.

1.q: Why do code links point at a commit rather than the branch?
1.a: Because the branch moves. A link to a file on main will point somewhere else next week, and the whole value of the link is that it shows the code as it was when the problem started.

2.q: Does a deployment before a problem mean it caused it?
2.a: No, and OpsWatch never says so. It says a deployment happened eight minutes earlier. That is a correlation, and it is yours to interpret.

ec2.title: Monitor EC2
ec2.summary: Instances by availability zone, coloured by the one signal that means broken.
ec2.what: OpsWatch lists your instances and reads their CloudWatch metrics. It colours an instance by its AWS status check — and deliberately not by CPU.

before.0: A connected AWS account with EC2 permissions allowed.

0.title: Open the host map
0.body: Instances, then Overview. Each instance is a tile, grouped by availability zone.

1.title: Understand the colour
1.body: Green means the AWS status check passed. Red means it failed. An outline means the instance is running and publishing no status check, so OpsWatch cannot vouch for it.

2.title: Understand what CPU is not
2.body: A batch host at 95% is doing its job; a web server at 95% may be in trouble. OpsWatch cannot tell which yours is, so CPU is shown, ranked and charted — never turned into a verdict.

3.title: Turn on detailed monitoring for finer data
3.body: Basic monitoring publishes every five minutes. Detailed monitoring publishes every minute and is billed by AWS.

ec2.verify: The host map groups your instances by zone and the summary names any zone where something could not be read.

0.q: Every instance is an outline.
0.a: No status-check metrics are reaching CloudWatch for them. Check that the instances are genuinely running and that the connection has CloudWatch permissions.

1.q: A stopped instance shows as healthy.
1.a: Stopping an instance is a decision somebody made. OpsWatch says it is stopped and does not treat that as a fault.

0.label: Why an outline is not a red square

ecs.title: Monitor ECS
ecs.summary: Clusters, services and tasks — and how to get the CPU and memory numbers.
ecs.what: OpsWatch reads your ECS clusters and services through the describe actions in the role, and their CPU and memory from CloudWatch. It colours a service by whether its tasks are running, what its utilisation is, and how its last deployment went.

before.0: A connected AWS account with ECS permissions allowed.

0.title: Open the ECS overview
0.body: Containers, then Overview. Every service is a tile, grouped by cluster.

1.title: Check the verdict
1.body: A service is healthy when its tasks are running, its CPU and memory are inside the band, and its last deployment completed. A service deliberately scaled to zero is healthy, not broken.

2.title: Turn on Container Insights if you want more
2.body: Basic CPU and memory arrive without it. Container Insights adds task-level counts and is enabled per cluster in the ECS console or with the CLI.

3.title: Point your logs at CloudWatch
3.body: Use the awslogs driver in your task definition so OpsWatch can search them and find errors.

ecs.verify: The ECS overview shows a verdict, the counts beside it, and the checks it ran — including the CPU and memory figures with the threshold they were compared against.

0.q: CPU and memory are empty.
0.a: The service publishes no utilisation metrics. That is normal for some launch types; OpsWatch lists only the checks that ran rather than inventing a zero.

1.q: A service shows 0 of 2 tasks running.
1.a: Nothing is serving. Look at the service events in the AWS console — the usual causes are an image that cannot be pulled, a failing health check, or no capacity.

0.label: Send logs so errors become problems

first-login.title: First login
first-login.summary: Create the administrator, then decide how people sign in.
first-login.what: The first person to open OpsWatch creates the administrator account. After that the setup page is closed and everybody signs in with a password, or with Google if you configure it.

before.0: OpsWatch installed and running.
before.1: A password manager, ideally. The password is not recoverable.

0.title: Create the administrator
0.body: Open OpsWatch and fill in the email and password. This happens once; afterwards the setup page answers "not found".

1.title: Sign in
1.body: Use the email and password you just chose.

2.title: Optionally, turn on Google sign-in
2.body: Set the Google client id, secret and public URL in the environment and restart. Sign-in configuration lives in the environment on purpose: a login provider that could be changed from inside the application would be a way to take the application over.

first-login.verify: You land on Connections. The Integrations page shows Google sign-in as connected if you configured it, and as not configured if you did not.

0.q: I forgot the administrator password.
0.a: There is no reset from inside the product. Stop the container, remove the admin row from the database in the data volume, and start again.

1.q: Is Google sign-in the same as connecting Google Cloud?
1.a: No. It is a way of signing in to OpsWatch. OpsWatch does not read anything from Google.

history.title: Keep history and build baselines
history.summary: Off by default, because it costs money. Here is what turning it on buys.
history.what: OpsWatch answers most questions from what AWS already keeps. Historical collection is for the questions that need yesterday: charts on a problem, baselines, reports and objectives.

before.0: A connected AWS account.
before.1: A view on how much CloudWatch querying you are willing to pay for.

0.title: Understand why it is off
0.body: Every collection cycle is a billed CloudWatch call. OpsWatch will not spend your money by default, so it ships with collection off and every page that would use it says so.

1.title: Turn it on
1.body: Settings, then Data and history. Choose an interval. The page states what each interval costs in calls per day.

2.title: Choose retention
2.body: Older points are rolled up rather than kept raw, so the database grows slowly and predictably.

3.title: Wait for a baseline
3.body: Baselines need enough history to be meaningful. Until there is enough, OpsWatch says there is not enough rather than comparing against a number it made up.

4.title: Back it up
4.body: Everything lives in the data volume. Snapshot the volume, and keep your OPSWATCH_SECRET with it — without the secret the stored credentials cannot be read.

history.verify: A problem detail shows a chart of the measured signal instead of the sentence explaining that history is off.

0.q: Where is the data stored?
0.a: In SQLite, inside the container’s data volume, on your machine. Nothing is sent anywhere.

1.q: I turned it on and the charts are still empty.
1.a: They fill from the moment you turn it on. OpsWatch does not backfill, because backfilling means paying to re-read a window you did not ask for.

2.q: How do I make OpsWatch keep statistics?
2.a: This is that guide. Turn on historical collection; baselines, reports and objectives all build on it.

install.title: Install OpsWatch
install.summary: One container, one volume, on a machine you control.
install.what: OpsWatch runs as a single container with one data volume. Everything it knows — your connections, your problems, your history — lives in that volume on your machine, and nothing is sent anywhere else.

before.0: A machine with Docker and Docker Compose installed.
before.1: A free port. The examples use 3111.

0.title: Get the compose file
0.body: Clone the repository, or copy docker-compose.yml from it.

1.title: Set the secret
1.body: OPSWATCH_SECRET encrypts every credential OpsWatch stores. Generate one and keep it: if you lose it, the stored credentials cannot be decrypted and you will have to reconnect everything.

2.title: Start it
2.body: The first start creates the database and applies every migration.

3.title: Open it
3.body: It binds to localhost only. To reach it from elsewhere, put it behind an HTTPS reverse proxy and set OPSWATCH_PUBLIC_URL — create your administrator account first.

install.verify: The sign-in page loads and asks you to create an administrator. If you see it, the container is running and the database is ready.

0.q: The page does not load.
0.a: Check the container is healthy with docker compose ps, then read docker compose logs opswatch. A missing OPSWATCH_SECRET is the usual cause.

1.q: Can I move it to another machine?
1.a: Yes. Copy the data volume and use the same OPSWATCH_SECRET. Without that secret the stored credentials are unreadable.

kubernetes.title: Monitor Kubernetes on EKS
kubernetes.summary: Container Insights is the whole story — what it gives you, and exactly where it stops.
kubernetes.what: OpsWatch reads Kubernetes through CloudWatch Container Insights. That needs no permission beyond the ones your role already has, and it is not on by default: until you enable it, OpsWatch cannot see your cluster and will say so rather than showing you a reassuring empty page.

before.0: An EKS cluster and permission to add an add-on to it.
before.1: A connected AWS account with CloudWatch permissions allowed.
before.2: Container Insights is billed by AWS as custom metrics. Check the cost for your cluster size before enabling it everywhere.

0.title: Enable Container Insights on the cluster
0.body: The simplest route is the CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on, which installs the agent for you.

1.title: Wait for metrics to appear
1.body: The first datapoints arrive within a few minutes. OpsWatch finds clusters by their node-count metric, so nothing appears until that is published.

2.title: Open the Kubernetes section
2.body: Every pod is a tile, grouped by namespace. Nodes and cluster health are beside it.

3.title: Read the boundary
3.body: The page carries a card saying what this view cannot see. It is worth reading once.

kubernetes.verify: The Kubernetes section shows your cluster, its nodes, and a tile for every running pod. If it still says no cluster is reporting, the metrics are not reaching CloudWatch yet.

0.q: It says no cluster is reporting, but I have one.
0.a: Container Insights is not enabled on it, or the agent cannot publish. OpsWatch cannot tell that apart from having no cluster, so it claims neither.

1.q: Why can I not see containers, only pods?
1.a: Container Insights aggregates to the pod. Per-container state lives in the kubelet and would need something running inside your cluster to read it.

2.q: A workload I know is broken does not appear.
2.a: This is the sharpest edge of reading Kubernetes from CloudWatch. A workload whose pods all failed to start publishes no pod metrics, so it looks the same here as a workload that does not exist. Events and pod phases are not in CloudWatch.

3.q: Would an in-cluster agent from OpsWatch fix that?
3.a: It would: events, pod phases, owner references and per-container state all need something inside the cluster. OpsWatch does not ship one. It is a real product with its own trust boundary — something running in your cluster, holding a credential, sending data out — and we will not pretend it exists.

0.label: Why missing telemetry is never green

logs.title: Send logs so OpsWatch can read them
logs.summary: CloudWatch Logs in, search and error grouping out.
logs.what: OpsWatch reads logs from CloudWatch Logs. It searches them when you ask, and it groups exceptions into errors that can become problems.

before.0: A connected AWS account with logs permissions allowed.

0.title: Send your logs to CloudWatch
0.body: On ECS, set the awslogs driver on the container definition. On EC2, install the CloudWatch agent. On Lambda it happens by itself.

1.title: Choose the log groups
1.body: Logs, then Sources. OpsWatch lists what it can see and you opt each group in. Nothing is queried until you do.

2.title: Search
2.body: Logs, then Search. Type what you are looking for — OpsWatch writes the query and shows it. AWS bills for the data a search scans, so fewer groups and a shorter range cost less.

3.title: Let errors group themselves
3.body: OpsWatch fingerprints exceptions by their type, their normalised message and the frames that matter — never by line number, so a blank line inserted above does not split a group in two.

logs.verify: The Errors page lists groups with a count and a first-seen time, and a search returns rows from your chosen groups.

0.q: No log groups are listed.
0.a: Either the logs permissions are denied, or nothing is writing to CloudWatch Logs in that region.

1.q: Queries feel expensive.
1.a: They are billed by data scanned. Narrow the time range and pick fewer groups; OpsWatch shows the estimate before you run one.

1.label: Turn an error into a line of code

problems.title: Problems, from opened to resolved
problems.summary: What a problem is, how it differs from an alarm, and how it closes.
problems.what: A problem is something OpsWatch measured and decided was worth your attention. It opens, it can come back, and it closes only when the measurement says so.

before.0: A connected AWS account with something running in it.

0.title: Read the first line
0.body: What it is, how serious, how long it has been going on, and where. If that line does not answer those four things, tell us.

1.title: Read what it affected
1.body: OpsWatch says "user impact not established" more often than not. That is the honest answer: it measures your estate, not your users.

2.title: Read why it opened
2.body: The measured value, the threshold it crossed, and the value it has to come back under.

3.title: Follow what to check
3.body: Each suggestion carries the evidence that produced it — a deployment eight minutes earlier, an error group that appeared nearby. An empty list is an answer too.

4.title: Let it close itself
4.body: A problem resolves after three consecutive clear readings over at least fifteen minutes. One quiet minute does not close anything.

problems.verify: Open a problem. You should see the verdict, the impact, the rule, what to check, possible causes, and a timeline of when it opened and whether it came back.

0.q: What is the difference between a problem and an alarm?
0.a: An alarm is a CloudWatch rule you wrote. A problem is a rule OpsWatch applied. An alarm in ALARM state becomes a problem, and OpsWatch will not invent causes for it — the rule is yours, not ours.

1.q: What is the difference between acknowledging and resolving?
1.a: Acknowledging says a person has seen it. Resolving is a measurement, and only the measurement can do it.

2.q: It says "Possible causes". Are those findings?
2.a: No. That card is the only thing on the page OpsWatch did not measure. It says so in its own words.

0.label: Connect code, so a problem can point at a commit

reading-status.title: Green, amber, red — and the two that are neither
reading-status.summary: What each colour means, and why OpsWatch refuses to show green it has not earned.
reading-status.what: Every resource OpsWatch shows has one of five states. Three of them are verdicts. Two of them are admissions, and they are the reason you can trust the other three.

before.0: Nothing. This is the one to read first.

0.title: Healthy means checked
0.body: Green says somebody looked, recently, and every check that ran passed. It never means "no problem row exists". The absence of a problem is the absence of evidence, not evidence of health.

1.title: Needs attention and Critical are measured
1.body: Amber and red come from a rule with a number in it. The problem page quotes that number and the threshold it crossed, so you can disagree with it.

2.title: Not evaluated means nobody looked
2.body: An outline with nothing in it. OpsWatch found the resource and has no reading for it — often because the telemetry it needs is not switched on.

3.title: Reading is old means we looked, a while ago
3.body: Same colour, different sentence. The last reading is too old to stand for what is happening now.

reading-status.verify: Open any infrastructure overview. Beside the verdict you will find the counts — how many are healthy, how many are not evaluated — and the list of checks that actually ran, with the age of the reading.

0.q: Everything says Not evaluated.
0.a: The telemetry OpsWatch needs is not reaching CloudWatch. Each section says which signal is missing and links to the guide for turning it on.

1.q: Why is a busy resource still green?
1.a: Because busy is not broken. OpsWatch only colours by signals that genuinely mean trouble — a failed status check, a saturated engine, tasks that are not running. High CPU on its own is shown, not judged.

redis.title: Monitor Redis on ElastiCache
redis.summary: Engine CPU, memory, evictions and hit rate — and which of them actually mean trouble.
redis.what: OpsWatch finds your Redis nodes through the metrics they publish to CloudWatch. It needs no ElastiCache permission and no stack redeployment. It judges two signals and shows several more without judging them.

before.0: A connected AWS account with CloudWatch permissions allowed.
before.1: At least one ElastiCache Redis node that has been running long enough to publish metrics.

0.title: Open the Redis section
0.body: Every node is a tile, grouped by cluster. Nothing to configure: if the nodes publish metrics, they are there.

1.title: Engine CPU is the one that matters
1.body: Redis runs its commands on a single thread. A four-core node can sit at 25% CPU with a completely saturated engine, which is why OpsWatch judges engine CPU and not CPU. AWS suggests alarming around 90%; OpsWatch warns at 75%.

2.title: Memory is about what happens next
2.body: As memory usage approaches 100%, Redis starts evicting keys, and past it writes fail. OpsWatch warns at 85% and calls it critical at 95%.

3.title: Evictions are a symptom, not an outage
3.body: A full cache evicting keys is a cache doing its job. OpsWatch warns so that you know, and does not treat it as a failure.

4.title: Hit rate and connections are shown, not judged
4.body: A cache deliberately holding only hot keys can run a low hit rate correctly, and OpsWatch cannot read your connection limit without the ElastiCache API. Both are numbers worth seeing and neither is a verdict.

redis.verify: The Redis section shows your cluster with a tile per node, and the node table shows engine CPU, memory, connections, evictions and hit rate. An idle cache shows no hit rate at all rather than zero per cent.

0.q: No Redis node is publishing metrics.
0.a: OpsWatch finds Redis through its engine CPU metric. A cluster that has just started, or one on an engine version old enough not to publish it, will not appear.

1.q: Engine CPU is high but CPU is low. Which is wrong?
1.a: Neither. That is the normal shape of a saturated Redis on a multi-core node, and it is exactly why the engine metric exists.

2.q: Why can I not see the node type or the replication setup?
2.a: Those come from the ElastiCache API, which is not in the role. OpsWatch reads what your nodes are doing, not what they are.

0.label: Be told when a cache fills up

searching-logs.title: Searching your logs
searching-logs.summary: Type what you are looking for. OpsWatch writes the query and shows it to you.
searching-logs.what: The Search page looks inside the log groups you choose and shows the lines that match. You do not need to know a query language: you type words, pick a level and a time range, and OpsWatch builds the CloudWatch Logs Insights query for you — and shows you exactly what it built.

1.label: Type what you are looking for

before.0: A connected AWS account whose permission test passes.
before.1: At least one log group with something in it. If you have none, read “Send logs so OpsWatch can read them” first.
before.2: Be aware that AWS bills for the data a search scans. Fewer log groups and a shorter range cost less.

0.title: Choose the log groups
0.body: The list on the left is bounded and scrolls on its own, so it never pushes the logs off the screen. Type in the box above it to filter the ones already loaded; if nothing matches, a button appears to ask AWS for more. The count under the box says how many you have ticked, and Clear unticks them all.

1.title: Type what you are looking for
1.body: Plain words, not a query: “timeout”, “500”, the name of a customer. Matching ignores capitals. Leave it empty to see everything in the range. You can also narrow by level, choose how far back to look, and choose how many lines to fetch.

2.title: Look at the query before you run it
2.body: Open “The query OpsWatch will run” to see exactly what will be sent to AWS. This is the query itself, not a description of it — you can copy it into a ticket, or click inside it to edit it by hand if you know Logs Insights.

3.title: Read the results
3.body: One line per record. The time is on the left, the level beside it when the line announces one, and the message fills the rest. Click a line to expand it and see every field, with a button to copy the message and a button to copy the whole record.

4.title: Narrow without searching again
4.body: The panel on the left counts the levels and the log streams in what came back. Clicking one filters the lines on screen — it does not run a second query, so it costs nothing and is instant.

5.title: Save a search you will run again
5.body: Give it a name and press Save. Saved searches are yours alone: nobody else sees them, nothing runs on its own, and nothing leaves this installation. Loading one is an ordinary navigation, so the browser’s back button undoes it and the address bar holds a link you can paste into a ticket.

searching-logs.verify: A search over a log group you know is busy returns lines with times in the range you chose, and the timeline above them has bars where those lines are.

0.q: It says the search ran and nothing matched.
0.a: That is exactly what it means, and it is not the same as “nothing was logged”. The search reached AWS, AWS looked, and no line in those groups and that range contained what you asked for. Try a shorter word, a wider range, or more log groups.

1.q: Why does it say “showing 100 of 4,213”?
1.a: You asked for 100 lines and 4,213 matched. Everything drawn from those lines — the count, the timeline, the level and stream counts — then describes the hundred you fetched rather than all of them, and the page says so. Raise the line count or narrow the search to close the gap.

2.a: Plenty of log lines do not say what level they are. OpsWatch leaves those blank and counts them as their own group. Colouring them “info” would be inventing a severity nobody wrote.

3.q: Nothing is listed on the left at all.
3.a: Either nothing is writing to CloudWatch Logs in this region, or the logs permissions are denied. OpsWatch cannot tell an empty log group from one it was not allowed to read, so it does not guess. Check the account’s permission test.

4.a: AWS bills Logs Insights by the data it scans, and a query over a day of a busy group scans a lot. Narrow the time range first, then the log groups. The note under the picker says the same thing.

5.q: Can the assistant search for me?
5.a: If an AI provider is configured, you can describe what you want and it will fill in the form. It proposes; it does not run. You see the five values it chose and the query they build, and the search starts only when you press Search. It can only choose from the log groups you already ticked, and it never sees a single log line.

1.label: Turn an error into a line of code

backup.title: Backing up, and putting a backup back
backup.summary: Everything OpsWatch knows is one file. Copy it somewhere else.
backup.what: OpsWatch keeps everything in a single SQLite file: your connections, your settings, the history it has collected and the problems it has found. Backing up means taking a copy of that file. OpsWatch takes one automatically before any upgrade that changes the database, and you can take one whenever you like.

before.0: Access to Settings, which means being signed in as the administrator.
before.1: Somewhere to keep the copy that is not the same disk as the original.
before.2: The value of OPSWATCH_SECRET from your .env file. You will need it to use the backup.

0.title: Check your data is on persistent storage
0.body: Settings, then Backup & restore. The top card says which directory the database is in and whether that directory survives a restart. If it says the directory is disposable, stop and fix that first — a backup of data that is about to vanish is not the problem you have.

1.title: Take a backup
1.body: Press Back up now. The file is written next to the database, and OpsWatch keeps the newest three. It is made by SQLite itself rather than by copying bytes, so it is a consistent file even though the database is in use.

2.title: Download it and put it somewhere else
2.body: Press Download beside a backup. A copy that lives on the same disk as the original is not a backup of that disk failing.

3.title: Keep OPSWATCH_SECRET with it — separately
3.body: The credentials inside are encrypted with that value, and it is deliberately not in the file. Without it, a restored instance starts but cannot reach AWS. With it, whoever has both has your instance. Keep the secret somewhere safe that is not the same place as the backup.

4.title: Putting one back
4.body: Stop OpsWatch. Copy the backup over opswatch.sqlite in the data directory. Delete the -wal and -shm files beside it. Start OpsWatch. The page gives you the exact commands.

backup.verify: The Backup & restore page lists the file with a size and a time, and downloading it gives a file your computer recognises as a database.

0.q: Why does OpsWatch not restore for me?
0.a: A running process cannot safely write over the database it has open. A restore button would sometimes half-succeed, which leaves you worse off than no restore at all: some of the old data, some of the new, and no way to tell which is which. Stopping OpsWatch first makes the operation boring, and boring is what you want from a restore.

1.q: Why delete the -wal and -shm files?
1.a: They are the write-ahead log of the database you just replaced. Left beside the restored file, SQLite will try to apply them to it and corrupt it. Deleting them is not optional.

2.q: I restored a backup and nothing can reach AWS.
2.a: OPSWATCH_SECRET is different from the value in use when the backup was taken. Every stored credential is encrypted with it, so with a different one they all fail to decrypt. Put the original value back, or reconnect each account.

3.a: Almost always the data directory is full or read-only. The page says which directory it is. OpsWatch never refuses to start because a backup failed — an upgrade you need is more important than a copy you can take afterwards — so check here rather than waiting to be told.

4.q: How often should I take one?
4.a: OpsWatch takes one before every upgrade that changes the database, which covers the risk it can see. The risk it cannot see is the disk, and that one is yours: take a copy off the machine as often as losing that much history would bother you.

0.label: Decide how much history to keep

api.title: Using the API
api.summary: Everything the pages show, as JSON. One token, one envelope, cursors for lists.
api.what: OpsWatch has a read-mostly HTTP API at /api/v1. It is the same data the pages render, in the same shapes, so a script you write against it cannot disagree with what you are looking at. There is no separate API key: you sign in with your own account and get a token.

before.0: An OpsWatch account. The API gives you exactly what your account can see, and nothing more.
before.1: The address of your instance, and a way to make an HTTP request — curl, a script, anything.

0.title: Get a token
0.body: POST your email and password to /api/v1/auth/login. The answer carries a bearer token. Send it as an authorization header on everything else. It is a session like any other, so you can see it and revoke it under your own sessions.

1.title: Find your environment id
1.body: GET /api/v1/environments lists them. Most endpoints want env=<connectionId>:<region>, which is the same pair in the address bar when you are looking at a page.

2.title: Read something
2.body: GET /api/v1/problems?env=… answers the same problems the Problems page shows. The body is the object itself: there is nothing to unwrap.

3.title: Page through a list
3.body: Pass limit and, after the first call, the nextCursor you were given. When nextCursor is null there is no more. Do not build a page number from it — it is a position, not an index.

4.title: Handle a failure once
4.body: Every failure is { "error": "<code>" } with an HTTP status to match. Write the handling once and it works for every endpoint, including ones added after your script was written.

api.verify: GET /api/v1/server answers without any credential at all, which makes it the quickest way to check you have the right address. Then GET /api/v1/me with your token answers who you are.

0.q: Is there an API key I can put in a config file?
0.a: No, and deliberately. A token belongs to an account, expires, appears in that account’s session list and can be revoked from it. An API key that lives in a file belongs to nobody and outlives everyone.

1.q: I get 401 on everything.
1.a: Either the token was not sent as authorization: Bearer <token>, or it has expired. Sessions roll over 12 hours. Sign in again.

2.q: I get 403 forbidden_origin from a browser.
2.a: A browser request arrived from an origin this instance does not serve. There is no CORS header on any endpoint on purpose: adding one would hand a page on another origin your session cookie. Call the API from a script or from this instance’s own pages.

3.q: Can I write through the API?
3.a: Only the few things the pages let you do: acknowledging an alert, dismissing an incident, changing your own preferences, revoking a session. OpsWatch is a read-only observer of your infrastructure, and the API is not a way around that.

4.q: Will an endpoint change under me?
4.a: The contract is additive. A field is added, never removed or renamed, and an unknown value from a newer server is designed to be readable rather than fatal. If that ever has to break, the version in the path is what changes.

0.label: Send alerts somewhere instead of polling

push-collection.title: Sending logs to OpsWatch as they happen
push-collection.summary: Optional. Off by default. OpsWatch reads AWS directly without it.
push-collection.what: OpsWatch normally reads your AWS account when it needs something: it assumes a read-only role and asks CloudWatch. That is the default and it stays the default. Managed collection is a second, optional way of getting log lines: a small Lambda in your account sends selected log groups to your OpsWatch instance as they are written. You enable it per account, you choose which log groups, and you can turn it off again without disconnecting anything.

before.0: A connected AWS account whose permission test passes.
before.1: OPSWATCH_PUBLIC_URL set to an HTTPS address AWS can reach. A laptop install cannot receive a webhook from Lambda.
before.2: Permission to run a second CloudFormation stack in that AWS account.
before.3: An understanding that AWS will charge for what it creates: Lambda invocations and duration, the forwarder’s own logs, and data transfer out of your account.

0.title: Decide whether you want it at all
0.body: You do not need it to see resources, read metrics, look at alarms or search existing logs. All of that works by reading AWS directly. Managed collection is for lines arriving continuously rather than when you ask — which is worth it if you want errors found within a minute instead of within fifteen.

1.title: Enable it on the account
1.body: Accounts, your account, then Managed collection. Read what it says, tick the confirmation, and press the button. Nothing is forwarded yet: this creates the possibility.

2.title: Copy the signing secret
2.body: It is shown once. It is what the Lambda uses to prove to your OpsWatch that a delivery is really from your forwarder. It is not an AWS credential and it grants no access to anything in your account.

3.title: Run the second stack
3.body: Download the collection template and deploy it, pasting the secret as the OpsWatchIngestSecret parameter. It is separate from the stack that connected the account, which is not touched. It creates a Lambda, a dead-letter queue, a role for the Lambda, a log group for it, and one policy attached to your existing OpsWatch role.

4.title: Verify it
4.body: Copy the ForwarderArn output back into OpsWatch and press Verify. OpsWatch asks AWS to confirm the function exists and reads the version the function itself reports, rather than believing what was typed.

5.title: Turn on real-time logs and choose your log groups
5.body: One at a time. OpsWatch never subscribes every log group in an account. Before it subscribes one it looks at what is already there, and refuses to replace another product’s forwarder.

6.title: Decide whether records are kept
6.body: Separately. Forwarding a line is not the same as storing it. With Keep forwarded records off, a line is processed and then discarded immediately — errors found in it survive, the line does not.

push-collection.verify: The forwarder card shows records accepted in the last hour and the time the last one arrived. Write a line to one of the log groups you chose and it should appear there within a minute.

0.q: Does connecting an AWS account send anything to OpsWatch?
0.a: No. A connected account is read directly and nothing leaves it. Managed collection is a separate switch, off by default, that you have to confirm — and even once it is on, nothing is forwarded until you pick a log group.

1.q: Does this send my data to some OpsWatch service?
1.a: There is no such service. OpsWatch is what you installed; the Lambda delivers to your own instance at your own address, which the page shows you. If you run OpsWatch on your own hardware, the data never leaves your network except to go from AWS to that address.

2.a: That is not a failure. It means no record has arrived and none has been refused — which is exactly what you expect from a quiet log group, out of hours, or a service that has not logged anything. It becomes Healthy the moment something arrives.

3.q: It says another product is already subscribed.
3.a: CloudWatch allows only a small number of subscription filters on a log group, and OpsWatch will not remove somebody else’s. It names the one that is in the way. Remove that filter if you want OpsWatch to have the slot, or forward a different log group.

4.q: AWS refused when I tried to start forwarding.
4.a: The permissions to manage subscription filters come from the collection stack, not the base one. Check that the collection stack deployed successfully and that the OpsWatchRoleName parameter matched your existing role.

5.a: OpsWatch will not invent a number, because AWS pricing depends on your account and region. What it does show is the usage: records accepted, refused and repeated, and bytes received, per hour. AWS charges for Lambda invocations and duration, the CloudWatch Logs the forwarder writes about itself, and data transfer out of your account.

6.q: How do I remove all of it?
6.a: Turn managed collection off — OpsWatch removes the subscription filters it created and forgets the secret — then delete the collection stack. Everything it made goes with it: the Lambda, its role, its log group and the queue. Nothing is retained. Your AWS connection and the base stack are untouched.

7.q: Who can read the signing secret?
7.a: It lives in the Lambda’s environment, so anyone in your AWS account with lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration can read it. That is worth knowing and is the trade-off of not requiring a secrets manager. It authenticates a forwarder to your OpsWatch; it is not an AWS credential. You can rotate it from the collection page and update the stack parameter.

connect-linux.title: Connect a Linux server
connect-linux.summary: Install a small agent on a machine, and OpsWatch can see its CPU, memory, load, uptime and disks — wherever it runs.
connect-linux.what: Cloud discovery finds what the cloud knows about. It does not find Redis installed on an Ubuntu box, a queue worker on a VPS, or a database on a machine under a desk. An agent does: it runs where the data is and reports out, so a machine behind NAT works like any other and OpsWatch never holds a credential that could log in to anything.

before.0: A Linux machine you can run commands on as root.
before.1: That machine must be able to reach this OpsWatch over HTTPS. OpsWatch never connects to it.
before.2: OPSWATCH_PUBLIC_URL set on this installation, so the agent has an address to report to.

0.title: Add the server
0.body: Linux servers, then Add a Linux server. Give it a name you will recognise. OpsWatch mints a key for this machine and shows it once.

1.title: Check what you are about to run
1.body: The command downloads the agent from this OpsWatch — not from the internet — and prints its SHA-256 before installing anything. Compare that with the checksum on the page. The agent is about a hundred lines of shell: /proc reads, one curl, one openssl.

2.title: Run it on the machine
2.body: As root. It installs the agent, writes the key to /etc/opswatch/agent.conf with mode 600, adds a cron entry, and runs once immediately.

3.title: Watch it appear
3.body: The machine shows up on the Linux servers page after its first report, usually within a minute, with what it is and what it measured.

connect-linux.verify: The server is listed as Reporting, and its page shows a CPU figure, a memory figure and its filesystems. A server that has been added but has not reported says Waiting for its first report — which is not the same as unhealthy, and not the same as stopped.

0.q: The server stays on “Waiting for its first report”.
0.a: Run /usr/local/bin/opswatch-agent by hand on the machine and read what it prints. The usual causes are a machine that cannot reach OPSWATCH_PUBLIC_URL, and a clock more than a few minutes out — the signature carries a timestamp, so a wrong clock is refused.

1.q: It says “Stopped reporting”.
1.a: Nothing has arrived recently, so nothing on the page is current. Check the cron entry at /etc/cron.d/opswatch-agent and run the agent by hand. OpsWatch cannot tell an agent that stopped from a machine that is unreachable, and does not guess.

2.q: CPU says “Not measured” on the first report.
2.a: A CPU percentage is a rate, and a rate needs two readings. The first report has nothing to compare against, so it says so rather than printing the since-boot average as though it were current.

3.q: Can OpsWatch run commands on the machine?
3.a: No. The agent opens no port and accepts nothing back. The key it holds proves which machine is reporting; it cannot log in, and there is no channel through which OpsWatch could ask a machine to do anything.

4.a: The kernel’s own counters — /proc/stat, /proc/meminfo, /proc/loadavg, /proc/uptime — and the output of df. It does not read process environments, file contents or anything you have not seen in the script.

5.q: How does it know Redis is running?
5.a: From a listening port and the name of the process holding it — and the page says exactly that, for every service it found. It is a guess, and OpsWatch shows you the guess rather than presenting it as a fact it checked. Where redis-cli is on the machine, the agent also runs INFO, which describes the server and never its contents: no key is read, no value is read, and KEYS is never run. If your Redis needs a password, put OPSWATCH_REDIS_PASSWORD in /etc/opswatch/agent.conf beside the key.

api.envelopeBody: A success returns the object itself. There is no { "data": … } wrapper to unwrap, and a list is { "items": [...], "nextCursor": … }.
api.authBody: A browser uses the session cookie it already has. Anything else posts to /auth/login and sends the token back as `authorization: Bearer <token>`. There is no separate API key.
api.pagingBody: A list takes `limit` and `cursor`, and answers with `nextCursor`. Pass it back to continue; `null` means there is no more. A page number would skip or repeat rows as the list changes underneath you.
api.timeBody: Every timestamp is a number of milliseconds since 1970 in UTC. A value that was not measured is null, never zero.
api.environmentBody: Pass `env=<connectionId>:<region>`. The environments you can use are listed by GET /environments.
api.example:
# Sign in once, keep the token.
TOKEN=$(curl -sS -X POST https://opswatch.example.com/api/v1/auth/login \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"you@example.com","password":"…"}' | jq -r .token)

# Then call anything with it.
curl -sS https://opswatch.example.com/api/v1/problems?env=6d293fe0d4b3:eu-west-1 \
  -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
api.errorsBody: Every failure of every endpoint answers { "error": "<code>" }, sometimes with `action` and `code` naming the AWS call behind it. Handle the shape once. An unknown code from a newer server is still readable, which is why it is a string rather than an enum.
api.endpointsBody: {count} of them, generated from the same list the routes are tested against — so this cannot describe one that is not there, or miss one that is. The codes under each summary are the failures beyond the ones every endpoint shares.
api.openapi: The machine-readable version of all of this:

errorMeanings.invalid_request: A parameter is missing, malformed, or not one of the values this endpoint accepts.
errorMeanings.invalid_cursor: The `cursor` was not one this server issued. Start the list again without one.
errorMeanings.invalid_credentials: The email or password was wrong. The same answer for both, on purpose.
errorMeanings.unauthorized: No credential was presented, or the one presented has expired.
errorMeanings.forbidden: The credential is valid but is not allowed to do this.
errorMeanings.forbidden_origin: A browser request arrived from an origin this instance does not serve.
errorMeanings.not_found: No such object, or none the caller is allowed to see. The two answer the same.
errorMeanings.method_not_allowed: That path exists with a different method.
errorMeanings.conflict: The object changed underneath the request, or already exists.
errorMeanings.rate_limited: Too many attempts. `Retry-After` says how long to wait.
errorMeanings.internal_error: OpsWatch failed. Every endpoint can answer this, so it is not listed on each one.
errorMeanings.aws_denied: AWS refused the call. `action` names the permission it wanted.
errorMeanings.aws_throttled: AWS is rate limiting this account.
errorMeanings.aws_error: AWS answered with an error. `code` carries its own.
errorMeanings.unavailable: A dependency this endpoint needs is not available right now.

Search.title: Search OpsWatch
Search.placeholder: A service, a problem, a guide…
Search.noResults: Nothing found. Try the name of the resource, or fewer words.
Search.hint: Arrows to move, Enter to open, Escape to close. Press / from anywhere.

Collection.title: Managed collection — {name}
Collection.description: Whether anything is sent from this AWS account to OpsWatch, and what.

mode.title: How OpsWatch reads this account
mode.hint: The first thing to know about any AWS connection.
mode.directHint: OpsWatch reads this account when it needs to, using the read-only role. Nothing is sent from your AWS account to anywhere.
mode.managedHint: Selected log groups are sent from your AWS account to this OpsWatch instance as they are written. Reading AWS directly continues exactly as before.
mode.destinationDirect: Nowhere — OpsWatch reads AWS, nothing is forwarded.
mode.noDestination: Not set. OPSWATCH_PUBLIC_URL must be an address AWS can reach.

enable.title: Enable managed collection
enable.hint: Off. Connecting an AWS account does not enable this, and never will.
enable.what: Selected log groups will be sent from your AWS account to this OpsWatch instance, over HTTPS, signed.
enable.creates: You will run a second CloudFormation stack that creates a small forwarder Lambda, a dead-letter queue and one policy. It is separate from your base stack, which is not touched.
enable.costs: AWS may charge for what that creates: Lambda invocations and duration, the CloudWatch Logs the forwarder writes about itself, and data transfer out of your account.
enable.nothingYet: Nothing is forwarded until you choose a log group. Enabling this creates the possibility, not the traffic.
enable.confirm: I understand that selected AWS log data will be sent to this OpsWatch instance.

Collection.secretHint: Copy it now. It is shown once and never again. You will paste it as the OpsWatchIngestSecret parameter when you deploy the stack. It authenticates the forwarder to this OpsWatch; it is not an AWS credential and grants no access to anything in your account.

regions.title: Which region
regions.hint: A forwarder lives in one region and can only be reached by subscription filters in that region, so each region of this account is set up separately.

install.title: Install the forwarder
install.hint: A second stack, separate from the one that connects the account.
install.deploy: Deploy it in {region}, pasting the secret when asked:
install.verifyStep: Copy the ForwarderArn output back here and verify it.
install.noSecretInTemplate: The template contains no secret. It can be read, diffed and kept; the secret is supplied when you deploy and lives only in the function’s environment.
install.perRegion: Each region is set up on its own: choose another above once this one is forwarding.

forwarder.title: Forwarder
forwarder.hint: What this instance has actually heard, over the last hour.
forwarder.deadLettersCount: {count, plural, =0 {None} one {# waiting in the dead-letter queue} other {# waiting in the dead-letter queue}}

verify.label: Forwarder function ARN
verify.hint: From the ForwarderArn output of the collection stack. OpsWatch asks AWS to confirm it rather than taking your word for it.

settings.title: What is collected, and what is kept
settings.hint: Two separate decisions. Forwarding data is not the same as storing it.
settings.realtimeHint: Allow selected log groups to be forwarded. With this off, nothing is accepted even from a correctly signed forwarder.
settings.persistOn: Records are kept for the window below and can be searched afterwards.
settings.persistOff: Records are processed and then discarded immediately. Errors found in them survive; the log lines do not.
settings.retentionHint: Only applies when records are kept. Nothing is retained longer than this.

groups.title: Log groups
groups.hint: One at a time. OpsWatch never subscribes an account’s every log group.
groups.sourceOff: Real-time logs is off, so nothing can be started. Switch it on above first.
groups.noneLeft: Every log group in this region is already listed above.
groups.unavailable: OpsWatch could not list the log groups of this region. Check the account’s permission test.
groups.truncated: Showing the first {count}. Forward the ones you need; this is not a list to work through.
groups.costs: AWS charges for what forwarding uses: Lambda invocations and duration, the forwarder’s own CloudWatch Logs, and data transfer out of your account. OpsWatch shows you the usage above rather than guessing at a price.

disable.title: Turn managed collection off
disable.hint: This does not disconnect the AWS account.
disable.subscriptions: Every subscription filter OpsWatch created is removed, so nothing new is sent.
disable.secret: The signing secret is forgotten, so anything already in flight cannot authenticate.
disable.records: Queued and kept records are dropped. Errors already found in them survive.
disable.keepsConnection: The AWS connection stays exactly as it is, and OpsWatch keeps reading it directly.
disable.confirm: I understand that forwarding will stop and OpsWatch-created subscriptions will be removed.
disable.removed: {count, plural, one {# subscription removed.} other {# subscriptions removed.}}
disable.failed: {count, plural, one {# could not be removed — delete it or the stack yourself, it is still costing invocations.} other {# could not be removed — delete them or the stack yourself, they are still costing invocations.}}
disable.stack: Then delete the collection stack. Everything OpsWatch created goes with it; nothing is retained.

errors.not_confirmed: Tick the confirmation to enable managed collection.
errors.no_public_url: Managed collection needs OPSWATCH_PUBLIC_URL set to an HTTPS address AWS can reach. A forwarder cannot deliver to an instance it cannot find.
errors.conflict: Another subscription filter is already on that log group.
errors.conflictWith: “{owner}” is already subscribed to that log group. OpsWatch will not replace another product’s forwarder. Remove it first, or forward a different group.
errors.limit: That log group already has as many subscription filters as AWS allows.
errors.denied: AWS refused. The collection stack grants the permissions this needs — check it is installed and up to date.
errors.not_found: That log group, or the forwarder, could not be found.
errors.failed: That did not work. Check the forwarder is verified and real-time logs is on.
errors.invalid_arn: That is not a Lambda function ARN.

rotate.hint: Issue a new signing secret. The current one stops working immediately, so update the stack parameter straight afterwards — between the two, the forwarder cannot deliver.

Hosts.title: Linux servers
Hosts.description: Machines OpsWatch watches directly, wherever they run.
Hosts.listHint: A server is a machine, not an attribute of a cloud account: it may be an EC2 instance, a Droplet, or a box under somebody’s desk.
Hosts.none: No Linux server has been enrolled yet.

enrol.title: Add a Linux server
enrol.hint: You install a small agent on the machine. It reaches out to OpsWatch; OpsWatch never reaches in.
enrol.whatItReads: The agent reads the kernel’s own counters — CPU, memory, load, uptime and disk usage — and posts them every five minutes.

guidance.title: What to check
guidance.hint: OpsWatch read one figure from this machine. These are things to look at, not a diagnosis of why.

checks.0: Which directory is holding it: sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 / | sort -h | tail, then the same one level down.
checks.1: Log files that nobody rotates. /var/log is the usual one, and a service writing its own log elsewhere is the usual surprise.
checks.2: Deleted files a process still has open — they keep their space until it closes them: sudo lsof +L1.
checks.3: Package caches and old kernels, which are safe to clear and often large.
checks.4: Whether the filesystem is the one you think. A full / and an empty /data look identical from an application's point of view until a write fails.

services.redis: Redis is running here. Check whether it is writing snapshots or an append-only file to this filesystem, and how large they have grown — dir and dbfilename in its config say where.
services.docker: Docker is running here. Images, stopped containers and unused volumes accumulate; docker system df says how much they hold.

checks.0: What is holding it: ps -eo pid,comm,rss --sort=-rss | head.
checks.1: Whether the kernel has already killed something for it — dmesg -T | grep -i oom — which would explain a service that restarted for no apparent reason.
checks.2: Whether there is swap, and whether it is being used. A machine with none goes from fine to killing processes with nothing in between.
checks.3: Whether the figure is cache rather than use. Linux counts page cache as used until something else needs it, and free -h separates them.

services.redis: Redis is running here. Check its used_memory against its maxmemory — with no limit set it will keep growing until the kernel intervenes, and the machine's memory is the only ceiling.

checks.0: Whether the machine is up at all. This says only that nothing has arrived from it.
checks.1: Whether the agent is still scheduled: its cron entry, and /etc/opswatch/agent.conf.
checks.2: Whether the machine can still reach this OpsWatch — a firewall change or a rotated address stops reports without touching the machine.
checks.3: Whether the secret still matches. A machine removed and re-enrolled here has a new one, and the old agent's reports are refused.

checks.0: Which directory is holding it: sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 / | sort -h | tail, then the same one level down.
checks.1: Log files that nobody rotates. /var/log is the usual one, and a service writing its own log elsewhere is the usual surprise.
checks.2: Deleted files a process still has open — they keep their space until it closes them: sudo lsof +L1.
checks.3: Package caches and old kernels, which are safe to clear and often large.
checks.4: Whether the filesystem is the one you think. A full / and an empty /data look identical from an application's point of view until a write fails.

services.redis: Redis is running here. Check whether it is writing snapshots or an append-only file to this filesystem, and how large they have grown — dir and dbfilename in its config say where.
services.docker: Docker is running here. Images, stopped containers and unused volumes accumulate; docker system df says how much they hold.

checks.0: Whether it is deliberate. On a machine that exists to run Redis, the machine's memory is the limit — and that is a decision, not a mistake.
checks.1: What happens when it reaches the machine's: with no maxmemory, Redis does not evict, so the kernel picks a process to kill and it is often Redis itself.
checks.2: Setting one, if it is not deliberate: maxmemory and a maxmemory-policy together decide what Redis gives up first, rather than leaving it to the kernel.
checks.3: Whether the growth is data you meant to keep. A cache with no expiry set on its keys grows without limit whatever the machine has.

checks.0: Which policy is set: redis-cli CONFIG GET maxmemory-policy. noeviction means writes start failing rather than keys being dropped.
checks.1: Whether it is already evicting: evicted_keys in INFO stats counts them since Redis started.
checks.2: Whether keys have an expiry. A cache whose entries never expire reaches any limit eventually.
checks.3: Whether the limit is still the right one for what this Redis now holds.

checks.0: Why, in Redis's own log — it records the reason it could not write the snapshot.
checks.1: Whether the filesystem it saves to has room. A failed save and a full disk are usually the same incident.
checks.2: Whether the directory is writable by the user Redis runs as: dir in its config says which directory.
checks.3: What this costs you if Redis restarts before the next successful save — everything written since the last one that worked.

GoogleWizard.title: Connect a Google Cloud project
GoogleWizard.description: OpsWatch reads the project. It never holds a credential for it.
GoogleWizard.accessTitle: What OpsWatch will be able to read
GoogleWizard.accessHint: These two roles and nothing else. Both are read-only, and both are Google's own predefined roles rather than something OpsWatch asks you to write.

roles.compute: the instances in the project, so OpsWatch can see what is running
roles.monitoring: the metrics Google already collects, so it can see how they are doing

GoogleWizard.noKey: No service account key is created, downloaded or stored.
